See how this bachelor compares with study options at UCR

This is a pre-produced programme comparison. Your search helped you find the programme; it did not personalize the comparison.

← Back to search

Erasmus University Rotterdam's Bachelor in Philosophy of a Specific Discipline combines 90 EC in a separate bachelor discipline with 60 EC of common philosophy, 15 EC of discipline-specific philosophy and a 15-EC milestones-and-thesis trajectory that integrates both fields.

Three UCR programmes offer related study through philosophy with economics and business, society and law, or health and human existence. Each has a substantial philosophy-and-ethics spine and a genuine second disciplinary strand, but none reproduces Rotterdam's full common philosophy sequence, verified discipline-specific philosophy package or required integrative philosophy thesis.

Academic year: 2026–2027

External pathway: Economics and Business Economics discipline route selected by neutral official-order tie-break

The governing 2026–2027 TER supplies the complete 180-EC structure. Exact discipline-specific philosophy assignments are MyEUR-only, so the required 15 EC is preserved without inventing a pair. The public page's detailed course guide is labelled 2025–2026 and is not merged into this cohort. Admission requires 60 EC from another recognised Dutch university bachelor; completion requires at least 90 EC from it; and starting the thesis trajectory requires 30 EC completed within BPSD.

What this comparison shows

A curriculum-level comparison of Philosophy of a Specific Discipline at Erasmus University Rotterdam with 3 illustrative UCR study compositions.

CLOSEST UCR MATCH
Philosophy, economics & business

The closest feasible response to the selected Economics and Business Economics route: philosophical study of knowledge, mind, ethics and political authority is combined with a substantial economics, business, finance, governance and research-methods sequence.

ADDITIONAL UCR OPTION
Philosophy, society & law

A programme organised around the philosophical examination of law, social institutions and global power: the philosophy core is combined with public, private, criminal, constitutional and EU law, plus sociology, international relations, conflict studies, history and argument.

ADDITIONAL UCR OPTION
Philosophy, health & human existence

A programme organised around philosophical questions of human existence, mind, health, illness and responsibility: ethics and metaphysics are combined with biomedical science, public health, psychology and evidence-based health research.

Important limitation

This is a curriculum comparison. A UCR composition is not the same disciplinary degree and does not by itself establish a professional qualification or automatic eligibility for a particular master’s programme.

Rows show curricular relationships, including partial matches, rather than course equivalence. A blank cell means there is no closely comparable component in that row. Optional independent research is additional to the displayed 180 EC.

modals.text:
Personal & Professional Development
This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
Close

Accounting & Corporate Finance
This course describes the most widely accepted accounting theory and practice with an emphasis on using and analyzing the information in financial statements. Students learn how to comprehend a typical corporate annual report and to use accounting as a tool in understanding how economic events affect business.
Close

Transnational Business Law
Businesses and entrepreneurs are confronted with legal complexity not only at the domestic level but particularly across divergent legal systems. This course presents a survey of the most essential fields of business law: contracts law, company law, trade law, intellectual property, and dispute resolution. An ultimate aim of the course is to critically examine the impact of globalization and digitization on the development of business law.
Close

Money, Banking & Finance
This course develops practical financial decision-making skills through case studies and real-world applications. Students learn to analyze financial data, assess risks, and make informed investment, budgeting, and business decisions that enhance value, financial security, and long-term planning.
Close

Introduction to Economics
Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
Close

International Macroeconomics
Study the economy as a whole through topics such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment. Understand how governments and central banks use fiscal and monetary policies to influence economic performance over time. The course also explores business cycles, international trade, and economic crises, preparing students to evaluate policy debates and global economic trends.
Close

Microeconomics & Behavior
Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.
Close

Public Economics
Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
Close

Econometrics
Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
Close

Behavioral Economics
This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.
Close

International Business & Governance
This course examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global businesses. It first explores how international companies operate, then centers on key global challenges including cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategies and global trade. It provides a comprehensive understanding of today’s complex international business environment.
Close

Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations
Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.
Close

Research Methods & Statistics
Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
Close

AI Ethics
AI Ethics examines artificial intelligence from philosophical and psychological perspectives. Topics include fairness and bias, privacy, responsibility, accountability, the moral status of AI systems and broader political risks. Students also consider trust and decision-making, empathy and confidentiality in clinical settings, algorithmic stereotypes, and how AI companions and tutors may affect children’s learning and relationships.
Close

Law, Society & Justice
Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.
Close

Histories of Gender
Explores lives of ordinary people through the lens of gender from the 19th to 21st centuries. Uses storytelling across cultural forms; topics include slavery, mid‑20th‑century life, conversion therapy, queer cinema and banned books; engages with projects like Walking With Pride.
Close

History Research Seminar
Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.
Close

Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
Close

Criminal Law & Criminal Justice
Examines moral and legal justifications for criminalisation and punishment. Investigates guiding principles of criminal law and justice, including criminal accountability, guilt, legality and fundamental principles, and applies theory through a simulated legal aid clinic.
Close

Introduction to Public International Law
Introduces rules, institutions and politics of public international law. Covers treaties, the UN, armed conflict, war crimes, refugee protection and climate change. Students analyse cases, debate issues and produce a podcast connecting law to global challenges.
Close

Comparative Constitutional Law
Explores constitutional law and state organisation, using a comparative approach. Covers constitutionalism, separation of powers, judicial review, federalism and fundamental rights, and discusses constitution‑making, religious constitutions and constitutional backsliding.
Close

Principles of Private Law
Examines principles of property law, tort law, contract law and other fields within private law. Uses comparisons of legal systems in four countries to explore rights and obligations arising from daily interactions.
Close

Foundations of European Union Law
Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.
Close

Introduction to Western Philosophy
Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers.
Close

Ethics
Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
Close

Philosophy of Mind
Examines historical and modern work on the philosophy of mind. Discusses Descartes’ dualism, the nature of consciousness, AI and animal minds, personal identity, transformative experiences and the influence of technology on experience.
Close

Philosophy of Emotion
Explores emotions from a philosophical perspective. Discusses nature and rationality of emotions, their role in ethics and art, and draws on historical and contemporary sources.
Close

Free Will, Time & the Self
Investigates concepts of free will, the role of luck and openness of the future. Explores relations between free will, time and the self across multiple modules and contemporary debates.
Close

Introduction to Political Philosophy
Introduces political philosophy. Examines concepts such as authority, freedom, equality, democracy, human rights, pluralism, multiculturalism, poverty and environmental issues through classical and contemporary texts. Emphasises essay writing and presentations.
Close

Theory of International Relations
Introduces basic theories of international relations and applies them to contemporary issues such as climate change, energy, humanitarian intervention, global crises and international relations between North-South and South-South actors. Includes a UN Security Council negotiation simulation.
Close

Peace & Conflict
Introduces Peace & Conflict Studies. Examines definitions of peace and conflict; analyzes conflict causation, violence typologies and radicalisation; applies reconciliation and conflict‑transformation models to real‑world scenarios through lectures and portfolio work.
Close

Introduction to Sociology
Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
Close

Qualitative Research Methodology
Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
Close

New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
Close

Epidemiology & Public Health
Introduces epidemiology and the evidence used in public health. It examines disease patterns, risks and changes over time, and how research can inform decisions about population health.
Close

Functional Anatomy
Introduces human body functioning using imaging, surface anatomy and dissection materials. Shows how anatomy serves function and discusses ethical considerations of learning from the dead.
Close

Pharmacology
Covers the science of drugs—their origin, composition, kinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity. Discusses drug targets, interactions and kinetics, enabling students to explain therapies in terms of molecular targets and physiological consequences.
Close

Infection & Immunity
Explores fundamental processes in immunology such as recognition of self vs non‑self, lymphocyte receptor development and innate and adaptive immune responses. Examines host‑pathogen interactions, inflammation, tissue damage and immunopathology.
Close

Mechanisms of Disease
Examines how normal organ-system function relates to disease. It connects embryology, anatomy and physiology with symptoms and failures in the cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, digestive, endocrine and central nervous systems.
Close

Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
Introduces cells, molecular biology, cellular physiology and communication. It connects genetic information and variation with living systems and offers initial perspectives on life sciences, biomedicine and public health. A research presentation develops engagement with scientific literature.
Close

Introduction to Brain & Behavior
Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
Close

Molecular Cell Biology
Provides foundation for practical applications in life science. Focuses on cellular biology of eukaryotes and prokaryotes, revisits concepts from introductory courses, examines current research and encourages evaluating reproducibility and modernising methods.
Close

Human Physiology
Studies normal functioning of the human body, covering structure‑function relationships, energy handling, homeostasis, signalling, organ systems and integration of their functions.
Close

Biochemistry
Explores the chemistry of life and biomolecules such as proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids. Discusses metabolic pathways, the role of biomolecules in health and disease and applications in medicine, biotechnology and sustainability.
Close

Life Science Laboratory
Introduces biochemical and molecular laboratory work. Covers themes like blood, proteins, bacteria, DNA and bioinformatics and provides a foundation for clinical and biomedical research.
Close

Molecular Pathology & Genetics
Covers general and molecular pathology and genetics. Studies cell injury, death, inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration, fibrosis and neoplasia, examines genetic mutations and diseases, and discusses genetic testing and ethical considerations.
Close

Social Psychology
Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.
Close

Abnormal Psychology
Provides a deep dive into factors shaping mental health. Teaches critical thinking, explores the bio‑psycho‑social approach and covers mental disorders, research findings and assessment techniques.
Close

Medical & Health Psychology
Uses a biopsychosocial approach to explore how biological, psychological and socio‑cultural factors influence health and illness. Covers theories, research and interventions and focuses on the role of psychological expertise in medical settings.
Close

Advanced Research Seminar
This course guides you through combining results from multiple studies using systematic reviews and meta-analysis a method now essential in psychology, medicine, social science and other disciplines. Want to know what really works? Gain hands-on skills in research synthesis that inform evidence-based policy and practice. You’ll search literature, manage data, and present findings that matter. Learn to calculate effect sizes, synthesize results and assess bias using R.
Close

Lifespan Developmental Psychology
Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.
Close

The Art of Rhetorical Communication
Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
Close

Persuasive Communication
Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
Close

The Rotterdam programme combines 90 EC from a separate chosen discipline with 60 EC of common philosophy, 15 EC of philosophy tailored to that discipline, and 15 EC of milestones and an integrative bachelor thesis. UCR instead combines individual philosophy courses directly with courses from economics and business, law and society, or health and biomedicine. UCR offers philosophy in ethics, mind, emotion, agency, political thought, human rights and AI, but it does not reproduce Rotterdam's dedicated analytic-philosophy, epistemology and philosophy-of-science sequence, its verified discipline-specific philosophy package, or a required thesis integrating philosophy with the chosen discipline.

Explore the UCR Program Builder ↗

modals.text:
Personal & Professional Development
This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
Close

Accounting & Corporate Finance
This course describes the most widely accepted accounting theory and practice with an emphasis on using and analyzing the information in financial statements. Students learn how to comprehend a typical corporate annual report and to use accounting as a tool in understanding how economic events affect business.
Close

Transnational Business Law
Businesses and entrepreneurs are confronted with legal complexity not only at the domestic level but particularly across divergent legal systems. This course presents a survey of the most essential fields of business law: contracts law, company law, trade law, intellectual property, and dispute resolution. An ultimate aim of the course is to critically examine the impact of globalization and digitization on the development of business law.
Close

Money, Banking & Finance
This course develops practical financial decision-making skills through case studies and real-world applications. Students learn to analyze financial data, assess risks, and make informed investment, budgeting, and business decisions that enhance value, financial security, and long-term planning.
Close

Introduction to Economics
Explore how individuals, firms, and societies make economic decisions. This course introduces key concepts from both microeconomics and macroeconomics, including markets, incentives, and the principles of supply and demand, and provides a foundation for analyzing real-world economic issues.
Close

International Macroeconomics
Study the economy as a whole through topics such as national income, economic growth, inflation, and unemployment. Understand how governments and central banks use fiscal and monetary policies to influence economic performance over time. The course also explores business cycles, international trade, and economic crises, preparing students to evaluate policy debates and global economic trends.
Close

Microeconomics & Behavior
Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.
Close

Public Economics
Investigate the role of government in the economy, focusing on how public policy influences efficiency and equity. The course covers taxation, public goods, externalities, and government spending. Combining theoretical models with empirical evidence, it evaluates how different policies affect societal welfare.
Close

Econometrics
Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
Close

Behavioral Economics
This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.
Close

International Business & Governance
This course examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global businesses. It first explores how international companies operate, then centers on key global challenges including cross-border governance, corporate responsibility, geopolitical strategies and global trade. It provides a comprehensive understanding of today’s complex international business environment.
Close

Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations
Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.
Close

Research Methods & Statistics
Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
Close

AI Ethics
AI Ethics examines artificial intelligence from philosophical and psychological perspectives. Topics include fairness and bias, privacy, responsibility, accountability, the moral status of AI systems and broader political risks. Students also consider trust and decision-making, empathy and confidentiality in clinical settings, algorithmic stereotypes, and how AI companions and tutors may affect children’s learning and relationships.
Close

Law, Society & Justice
Examines law from legal, socio‑scientific and normative perspectives. Explores definitions, legal traditions and fields of law, investigates the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and includes case law, excursion to international legal organisations, interviews with practitioners and a moot court session.
Close

Histories of Gender
Explores lives of ordinary people through the lens of gender from the 19th to 21st centuries. Uses storytelling across cultural forms; topics include slavery, mid‑20th‑century life, conversion therapy, queer cinema and banned books; engages with projects like Walking With Pride.
Close

History Research Seminar
Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.
Close

Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
Close

Criminal Law & Criminal Justice
Examines moral and legal justifications for criminalisation and punishment. Investigates guiding principles of criminal law and justice, including criminal accountability, guilt, legality and fundamental principles, and applies theory through a simulated legal aid clinic.
Close

Introduction to Public International Law
Introduces rules, institutions and politics of public international law. Covers treaties, the UN, armed conflict, war crimes, refugee protection and climate change. Students analyse cases, debate issues and produce a podcast connecting law to global challenges.
Close

Comparative Constitutional Law
Explores constitutional law and state organisation, using a comparative approach. Covers constitutionalism, separation of powers, judicial review, federalism and fundamental rights, and discusses constitution‑making, religious constitutions and constitutional backsliding.
Close

Principles of Private Law
Examines principles of property law, tort law, contract law and other fields within private law. Uses comparisons of legal systems in four countries to explore rights and obligations arising from daily interactions.
Close

Foundations of European Union Law
Introduces the EU legal order. Studies institutions, framework, citizenship and the internal market using problem‑based exercises and guest lectures.
Close

Introduction to Western Philosophy
Introduces central themes from Western philosophy over 2,500 years. Encourages inquiry into the significance of philosophical issues and their relation to other disciplines and teaches theoretical methods used by philosophers.
Close

Ethics
Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
Close

Philosophy of Mind
Examines historical and modern work on the philosophy of mind. Discusses Descartes’ dualism, the nature of consciousness, AI and animal minds, personal identity, transformative experiences and the influence of technology on experience.
Close

Philosophy of Emotion
Explores emotions from a philosophical perspective. Discusses nature and rationality of emotions, their role in ethics and art, and draws on historical and contemporary sources.
Close

Free Will, Time & the Self
Investigates concepts of free will, the role of luck and openness of the future. Explores relations between free will, time and the self across multiple modules and contemporary debates.
Close

Introduction to Political Philosophy
Introduces political philosophy. Examines concepts such as authority, freedom, equality, democracy, human rights, pluralism, multiculturalism, poverty and environmental issues through classical and contemporary texts. Emphasises essay writing and presentations.
Close

Theory of International Relations
Introduces basic theories of international relations and applies them to contemporary issues such as climate change, energy, humanitarian intervention, global crises and international relations between North-South and South-South actors. Includes a UN Security Council negotiation simulation.
Close

Peace & Conflict
Introduces Peace & Conflict Studies. Examines definitions of peace and conflict; analyzes conflict causation, violence typologies and radicalisation; applies reconciliation and conflict‑transformation models to real‑world scenarios through lectures and portfolio work.
Close

Introduction to Sociology
Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
Close

Qualitative Research Methodology
Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
Close

New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
Close

Epidemiology & Public Health
Introduces epidemiology and the evidence used in public health. It examines disease patterns, risks and changes over time, and how research can inform decisions about population health.
Close

Functional Anatomy
Introduces human body functioning using imaging, surface anatomy and dissection materials. Shows how anatomy serves function and discusses ethical considerations of learning from the dead.
Close

Pharmacology
Covers the science of drugs—their origin, composition, kinetics, therapeutic use and toxicity. Discusses drug targets, interactions and kinetics, enabling students to explain therapies in terms of molecular targets and physiological consequences.
Close

Infection & Immunity
Explores fundamental processes in immunology such as recognition of self vs non‑self, lymphocyte receptor development and innate and adaptive immune responses. Examines host‑pathogen interactions, inflammation, tissue damage and immunopathology.
Close

Mechanisms of Disease
Examines how normal organ-system function relates to disease. It connects embryology, anatomy and physiology with symptoms and failures in the cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, digestive, endocrine and central nervous systems.
Close

Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
Introduces cells, molecular biology, cellular physiology and communication. It connects genetic information and variation with living systems and offers initial perspectives on life sciences, biomedicine and public health. A research presentation develops engagement with scientific literature.
Close

Introduction to Brain & Behavior
Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
Close

Molecular Cell Biology
Provides foundation for practical applications in life science. Focuses on cellular biology of eukaryotes and prokaryotes, revisits concepts from introductory courses, examines current research and encourages evaluating reproducibility and modernising methods.
Close

Human Physiology
Studies normal functioning of the human body, covering structure‑function relationships, energy handling, homeostasis, signalling, organ systems and integration of their functions.
Close

Biochemistry
Explores the chemistry of life and biomolecules such as proteins, sugars, lipids and nucleic acids. Discusses metabolic pathways, the role of biomolecules in health and disease and applications in medicine, biotechnology and sustainability.
Close

Life Science Laboratory
Introduces biochemical and molecular laboratory work. Covers themes like blood, proteins, bacteria, DNA and bioinformatics and provides a foundation for clinical and biomedical research.
Close

Molecular Pathology & Genetics
Covers general and molecular pathology and genetics. Studies cell injury, death, inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration, fibrosis and neoplasia, examines genetic mutations and diseases, and discusses genetic testing and ethical considerations.
Close

Social Psychology
Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.
Close

Abnormal Psychology
Provides a deep dive into factors shaping mental health. Teaches critical thinking, explores the bio‑psycho‑social approach and covers mental disorders, research findings and assessment techniques.
Close

Medical & Health Psychology
Uses a biopsychosocial approach to explore how biological, psychological and socio‑cultural factors influence health and illness. Covers theories, research and interventions and focuses on the role of psychological expertise in medical settings.
Close

Advanced Research Seminar
This course guides you through combining results from multiple studies using systematic reviews and meta-analysis a method now essential in psychology, medicine, social science and other disciplines. Want to know what really works? Gain hands-on skills in research synthesis that inform evidence-based policy and practice. You’ll search literature, manage data, and present findings that matter. Learn to calculate effect sizes, synthesize results and assess bias using R.
Close

Lifespan Developmental Psychology
Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.
Close

The Art of Rhetorical Communication
Teaches how to craft persuasive messages, influence opinions, inspire action and connect people. Draws on historical communicators from Aristotle to Barack Obama and applies stylistic techniques to students’ own writing and speaking.
Close

Persuasive Communication
Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
Close
